nodes.name: Oaks & hickories
nodes.desc: Wikipedia classes the park's natural vegetation as oak/hickory forest. Their leaves, acorns and nuts feed many forest animals, and their litter feeds the soil.

nodes.name: American beech
nodes.desc: A hardwood common in the park's forest. Its nuts and leaves are eaten by deer and mice, with GloBI records for both.

nodes.name: Pawpaw
nodes.desc: A woodland understory tree with large fruit. GloBI records show raccoons and opossums eating it.

nodes.name: Spring wildflowers
nodes.desc: Trilliums, mayapple, phlox and other woodland flowers that carpet the forest floor in spring and are recorded often in the park.

nodes.name: White-tailed deer
nodes.desc: Often seen along park roads. Browses leaves, wildflowers and nuts, and is eaten by coyotes and scavenged by vultures.

nodes.name: Eastern gray squirrel
nodes.desc: Common in the park's hardwood forest. Eats acorns and nuts, and is prey for coyotes and snakes.

nodes.name: White-footed mouse
nodes.desc: A small forest rodent that eats seeds and nuts. Wikipedia says it is the most common prey of the timber rattlesnake.

nodes.name: Banded tussock moth
nodes.desc: Its caterpillars chew leaves of oak and many other trees. The adult moths are food for bats; GloBI records the red bat eating them.

nodes.name: Mammoth Cave cricket
nodes.desc: Eats whatever it can find. Wikipedia says its guano, eggs and carcasses feed many cave communities.

nodes.name: Mammoth Cave crayfish
nodes.desc: An eyeless crayfish of cave streams, named for the park. Cave crayfish generally scavenge leaf litter and detritus washed in from above.

nodes.name: Indiana bat
nodes.desc: The most recorded mammal near the park. Eats only flying insects such as moths and beetles and hibernates in cold caves.

nodes.name: Gray bat
nodes.desc: Roosts in limestone caves and hunts insects over rivers and riverside forest.

nodes.name: Northern cavefish
nodes.desc: An eyeless fish of caves in Kentucky and southern Indiana. Related cavefish eat small crustaceans, so crayfish are likely prey.

nodes.name: Central ratsnake
nodes.desc: Adults eat small mammals, birds and eggs. Wikipedia says black rat snakes also prey on hibernating Indiana bats.

nodes.name: Raccoon
nodes.desc: An omnivore that eats fruit like pawpaw, crayfish and other small animals, and takes hibernating bats.

nodes.name: Turkey vulture
nodes.desc: Among the most recorded birds near the park. Scavenges carcasses such as deer and other mammals.

nodes.name: Coyote
nodes.desc: Top mammal predator in the region. GloBI records it eating deer, squirrels, mice, rabbits and raccoons.

nodes.name: Timber rattlesnake
nodes.desc: Ambush predator of deciduous forest that winters in limestone crevices. Eats mostly small mammals, especially mice.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Spring light reaching the forest floor before the canopy leafs out powers the wildflowers and trees.

nodes.name: Rainfall
nodes.desc: Rain feeds the Green River and the sinking streams that flow into the cave system.

nodes.name: Karst limestone soil
nodes.desc: The park sits on a forested karst landscape of limestone, with sinkholes, caves and thin soils.

nodes.name: Fungi, beetles & bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down leaf litter, carcasses and cave guano and return nutrients to the soil.
